newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Double dose of supply dominates.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Double dose of supply dominates.

text.p: UK gilts are set for a busy week with two auctions to digest, key retail sales data due and the possibility of a U.S. interest rate rise to upset the applecart, analysts said on Monday.

Top of the list for the British bond market will be the two gilt auctions. The Bank of England will sell 1.5 billion stg of 7.0 percent gilts due 2002 on Tuesday and the same amount of the 8.0 percents of 2021 on Thursday.

"With such a small amount to be auctioned and the tone of the market so buoyant, both these auctions should be well covered with small tails," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale in London.

Nonetheless, having seen the gilt/Bund spread shoot in from 175 basis points before the May Day election to below 140 basis points last week, further outperformance may be out of reach for now. The spread stood at 143 on Monday.
"Profit-taking below 140 basis points should prevent the spread tightening significantly this week," Hilliard said.
Performance relative to U.S. Treasury bonds is entirely dependent upon what the Federal Open Market decides to do with U.S. interest rates on Tuesday.

"We now think the Fed will delay the next rate hike until the July 2 meeting," Hilliard said. "Although this should be positive for the market, the perception will remain that the Fed are merely waiting for the next meeting before acting."
On the economic data front, M4 broad money supply figures on Wednesday will be overshadowed by Wednesday's retail sales figures.
Economists forecast a 0.3 percent rise in sales, leaving them 4.1 percent higher than in April last year -- steady but not spectacular growth.

"The CBI distributive trades survey was consistent with a healthy expansion in retail sales activity during April, particularly for furniture and clothing retailers," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.

Windfall payments from the Alliance & Leicester's conversion into a bank and the one penny income tax announced in last November's budget would have boosted spending, he said. But the April 1 election may have led consumers to defer some big spending decisions.
Revised first quarter GDP figures will be released in tandem with the sales data while the Confederation of British Industry will put out its monthly trends survey later on Thursday.

The week got off to a bond-friendly start with April public sector borrowing figures showing 36 million stg of debt was repaid in the first month of the financial year. Economists had forecast a borrowing requirement of 1.7 billion stg.
But, in what could be a hint of the shape of things to come, gilts refused to rally. The June future was 5/32 lower at 113-20 half way through Monday's session.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, said the sharp flattening of the gilt curve that has accompanied the market's rally over the last fortnight, could have run its course.
He said the 25-year, ultra-long gilt, now yielding 7.14 percent, was only 20 basis points above the interest rate level implied by the December short sterling future.
"The short end of the yield curve is anchored by the prospect that base rates will rise to about 6.75 percent in the coming months," he said.

"With little chance of a sizeable curve inversion, and the likelihood of upward yield pressure in other major bond markets, we doubt that the absolute level of gilt yields will fall significantly further this year."
December short sterling, at 93.05 on Monday, is pricing in a half-point rise in 6.25 percent base rates by the year-end.
But Hilliard at SocGen saw some percentage in sticking with flattening trades. "The curve should flatten further on good news which may not happen until nearer to the mini-budget."

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will hold a mini-budget within weeks. Most economists say a significant fiscal tightening is needed to take the heat out of the domestic economy and take the pressure off monetary policy.

That could help short sterling too, Hilliard said. "Potentially the biggest opportunity for a (short sterling) rally in the coming weeks is a tight mini-budget which would take some of the pressure of monetary policy," he said.
